# Summary: Education in Germany
Germany's education system is largely decentralized, with each federal state (Land) responsible for its own schooling system. Secondary education is split into different tracks—Gymnasium (university-preparatory), Realschule (intermediate), Hauptschule (vocational preparation), Gesamtschule (comprehensive), and Sonderschule (special education). Gymnasium leads to the Abitur exam and higher education entrance, typically lasting until grade 12 or 13. Vocational education is strongly emphasized through the dual system (Duale Ausbildung), blending part-time vocational school with in-company apprenticeships. About 9.2% of students attend private schools, which are publicly funded and subject to government standards.
German tertiary education includes universities (Universitäten), which confer doctorates and emphasize research, and Universities of Applied Sciences (Fachhochschulen), focusing on practical skills and employability. Public universities generally charge low or no tuition fees, with semester fees covering administrative costs. Higher education degrees have transitioned to Bologna-system bachelor's and master's degrees, although traditional Diplom and Staatsexamen degrees remain for some fields. University admissions typically require the Abitur or equivalent qualifications, with various admissions procedures including local and nationwide restrictions. International students comprise around 15% of the student body. Academic achievement is influenced by social class and immigrant status, with ongoing debates regarding early student tracking and educational equity.
